claim: The yeast Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (TORC1) plays a central role in controlling growth.
source: The yeast Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (TORC1) plays a central role in controlling growth.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the general scientific consensus on TORC1 function.

claim: The signal triggering Rag/Gtr-dependent TORC1 activation upon amino-acid uptake is the coupled H+ influx catalyzed by amino-acid/H+ symporters.
source: We here report that the signal triggering Rag/Gtr-dependent TORC1 activation upon amino-acid uptake is the coupled H+ influx catalyzed by amino-acid/H+ symporters.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: H+-dependent uptake of other nutrients activates TORC1.
source: H+-dependent uptake of other nutrients, ionophore-mediated H+ diffusion, and inhibition of the vacuolar V-ATPase also activate TORC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing TORC1 activation upon uptake of various nutrients.

claim: Ionophore-mediated H+ diffusion activates TORC1.
source: H+-dependent uptake of other nutrients, ionophore-mediated H+ diffusion, and inhibition of the vacuolar V-ATPase also activate TORC1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing TORC1 activation upon FCCP treatment.

claim: Inhibition of the vacuolar V-ATPase activates TORC1.
source: H+-dependent uptake of other nutrients, ionophore-mediated H+ diffusion, and inhibition of the vacuolar V-ATPase also activate TORC1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing TORC1 activation upon treatment with V-ATPase inhibitors.

claim: The increase in cytosolic H+ elicited by H+ influx processes stimulates the compensating H+-export activity of the plasma membrane H+-ATPase (Pma1).
source: As the increase in cytosolic H+ elicited by these processes stimulates the compensating H+-export activity of the plasma membrane H+-ATPase (Pma1), we have examined whether this major ATP-consuming enzyme might be involved in TORC1 control.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Pma1 function and its response to cytosolic pH changes.

claim: When the endogenous Pma1 is replaced with a plant H+-ATPase, H+ influx or increase fails to activate TORC1.
source: We find that when the endogenous Pma1 is replaced with a plant H+-ATPase, H+ influx or increase fails to activate TORC1.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by experimental data comparing cells expressing Pma1 versus the plant H+-ATPase.

claim: Pma1 is a key actor in the mechanism of TORC1 activation by H+ influx coupled to nutrient uptake.
source: Our results show that H+ influx coupled to nutrient uptake stimulates TORC1 activity and that Pma1 is a key actor in this mechanism.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing the requirement of Pma1 for TORC1 activation.

claim: TORC1 operates by integrating upstream signals such as growth factors and nutrients to modulate multiple downstream effectors by phosphorylation.
source: It operates by integrating upstream signals such as growth factors (GFs) and nutrients to modulate, by phosphorylation, multiple downstream effectors, mostly proteins involved in anabolic processes (e.g. protein synthesis, ribosome biogenesis) or catabolic processes (e.g. autophagy, bulk endocytosis of plasma membrane transporters) (González and Hall, 2017; Powis and De Virgilio, 2016; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature establishing TORC1 function.

claim: mTORC1 dysfunction is associated with diseases including cancers.
source: The central role of TORC1 in regulating cell growth is illustrated by the many reported cases of mTORC1 dysfunction associated with diseases including cancers (Eltschinger and Loewith, 2016; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on mTORC1 and disease.

claim: In human cells, growth factors and amino acids are key signals of mTORC1 regulation.
source: In human cells, GFs and amino acids are key signals of mTORC1 regulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of mTORC1 regulation.

claim: Growth factors act through activation of Rheb, a GTPase present at the lysosomal membrane that stimulates mTORC1 activity.
source: GFs act through activation of Rheb, a GTPase present at the lysosomal membrane that stimulates mTORC1 activity (Durán and Hall, 2012; Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on Rheb and mTORC1.

claim: Amino acids such as leucine and arginine act via a complex of two GTPases (RagA or B and RagC or D) to promote recruitment of mTORC1 to the lysosome.
source: Amino acids such as leucine and arginine act via a complex of two GTPases, namely RagA or B and RagC or D, to promote recruitment of mTORC1 to the lysosome, where it is activated by Rheb.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited literature.

claim: The heterodimeric Rag GTPase complex recruits mTORC1 to the lysosome when RagA/B is bound to GTP and RagC/D to GDP.
source: The heterodimeric Rag GTPase complex recruits mTORC1 to the lysosome when RagA/B is bound to GTP and RagC/D to GDP (Kim et al., 2008; Sancak et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on Rag GTPases.

claim: Sestrin and Castor proteins act as cytosolic leucine and arginine sensors, respectively.
source: Importantly, Sestrin and Castor proteins have recently been found to act, respectively, as cytosolic leucine and arginine sensors.
evidence: This is supported by recent literature on amino acid sensing.

claim: When Sestrin and Castor proteins are bound to their specific amino acids, they lose the ability to inhibit GATOR2, resulting in TORC1 activation.
source: When bound to their specific amino acids, these sensor proteins lose the ability to inhibit GATOR2, a negative modulator of the GATOR1 GAP complex which inhibits RagA/B, and this results in TORC1 activation (Wolfson and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature on amino acid sensing mechanisms.

claim: Specific lysosomal amino acid transporters and the V-ATPase complex contribute importantly to mTORC1 control.
source: Specific lysosomal amino acid transporters and the V-ATPase complex also contribute importantly to mTORC1 control (Goberdhan et al., 2016; Zoncu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The TOR kinase that is part of TORC1 was originally identified in yeast after isolation of dominant TOR mutations conferring resistance to rapamycin.
source: The TOR kinase that is part of TORC1 was originally identified in yeast, after isolation of dominant TOR mutations conferring resistance to rapamycin (Rap) (Heitman et al., 1991; Loewith and Hall, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original discovery of TOR.

claim: The protein components of TORC1, the RagA/B and C/D proteins, and their upstream GATOR-type regulatory complexes exist in yeast.
source: The protein components of TORC1, the RagA/B and C/D proteins, and their upstream GATOR-type regulatory complexes also exist in yeast (Hatakeyama and De Virgilio, 2016; Loewith and Hall, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on yeast TORC1 components.

claim: RagA/B and RagC/D correspond to the yeast Gtr1 and Gtr2 proteins, respectively.
source: For instance, RagA/B and RagC/D correspond, respectively, to the yeast Gtr1 and Gtr2 proteins, which are part of a vacuole-associated complex (EGO) (Dubouloz et al., 2005) similar to the Rag-binding Ragulator of human cells (Sancak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on yeast Rag homologs.

claim: When cells are grown in nutrient-rich medium, yeast TORC1 is active and stimulates by phosphorylation a wide variety of proteins.
source: When cells are grown in nutrient-rich medium, yeast TORC1 is active and stimulates by phosphorylation a wide variety of proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TORC1 function in yeast.

claim: Active TORC1 stimulates the Sch9 kinase under conditions promoting anabolic functions and cell growth.
source: It notably stimulates the Sch9 kinase (Urban et al., 2007) under conditions promoting anabolic functions and cell growth.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on Sch9 regulation.

claim: Active TORC1 inhibits the Tap42-PP2A phosphatase, which stimulates autophagy, stress resistance, and nitrogen transport and utilization.
source: Active TORC1 also inhibits the Tap42-PP2A phosphatase, which stimulates autophagy, stress resistance, and nitrogen (N) transport and utilization (Loewith and Hall, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on TORC1 and Tap42-PP2A.

claim: TORC1 is inhibited in N-starved and Rap-treated cells.
source: In contrast, TORC1 is inhibited in N-starved and Rap-treated cells, so that anabolic processes, including protein synthesis, are inhibited and cell responses such as autophagy, bulk endocytosis of transporters, utilization of secondary N sources, and stress resistance are stimulated (Hatakeyama and De Virgilio, 2016; Loewith and Hall, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on TORC1 inhibition.

claim: The protein kinase Npr1 is a Tap42-PP2A target protein that is phospho-inhibited when TORC1 is active.
source: One Tap42-PP2A target protein is the protein kinase Npr1 (Nitrogen permease reactivator 1), which is phospho-inhibited when TORC1 is active (Schmidt et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on Npr1 regulation.

claim: Once Npr1 is inhibited, various permeases of nitrogenous compounds undergo intrinsic inactivation or downregulation via ubiquitylation, endocytosis, and degradation.
source: Once Npr1 is inhibited, various permeases of nitrogenous compounds undergo intrinsic inactivation (Boeckstaens et al., 2014; Boeckstaens et al., 2015) or downregulation via ubiquitylation, endocytosis, and degradation (MacGurn et al., 2011; Merhi and AndreAndré, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on permease regulation.

claim: Stimulation of TORC1 activity in yeast is usually monitored by visualizing the degree of Sch9 and/or Npr1 kinase phosphorylation.
source: Stimulation of TORC1 activity in yeast is usually monitored by visualizing the degree of Sch9 and/or Npr1 kinase phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established methodology in the field.

claim: Sch9 and Npr1 are moderately phosphorylated in cells grown on a poor N source such as proline, but hyperphosphorylated upon addition of a preferential N source such as glutamine or NH4+.
source: Sch9 and Npr1 are moderately phosphorylated in cells grown on a poor N source such as proline, but hyperphosphorylated upon addition of a preferential N source such as glutamine (Gln) or NH4+ (Schmidt et al., 1998; Stracka et al., 2014; Urban et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on TORC1 activity monitoring.

claim: Addition of any amino acid to proline-grown cells results in rapid but transient Rag/Gtr-dependent TORC1 activation.
source: In a study using Sch9 phosphorylation as readout, addition of any amino acid to proline-grown cells was found to result in rapid but transient Rag/Gtr-dependent TORC1 activation, whereas longer term TORC1 activation was observed only upon addition of an N source supporting optimal growth, for example Gln or NH4+, and it appeared not to depend on the Rag GTPases (Stracka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Longer term TORC1 activation is observed only upon addition of an N source supporting optimal growth and appears not to depend on the Rag GTPases.
source: In a study using Sch9 phosphorylation as readout, addition of any amino acid to proline-grown cells was found to result in rapid but transient Rag/Gtr-dependent TORC1 activation, whereas longer term TORC1 activation was observed only upon addition of an N source supporting optimal growth, for example Gln or NH4+, and it appeared not to depend on the Rag GTPases (Stracka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Sustained activation of TORC1 in response to NH4+ is impaired in mutant cells lacking the glutamate dehydrogenases involved in assimilation of NH4+ into amino acids.
source: Furthermore, sustained activation of TORC1 in response to NH4+ is impaired in mutant cells lacking the glutamate dehydrogenases involved in assimilation of NH4+ into amino acids (Fayyad-Kazan et al., 2016; Merhi and AndreAndré, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Glutamine behaves as a key signal for sustained TORC1 stimulation.
source: For instance, although Gln behaves as a key signal for sustained TORC1 stimulation (Crespo et al., 2002; Stracka et al., 2014), no Gln sensor has been identified to date, and yeast seems to lack Sestrin and Castor proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: No glutamine sensor has been identified in yeast to date.
source: For instance, although Gln behaves as a key signal for sustained TORC1 stimulation (Crespo et al., 2002; Stracka et al., 2014), no Gln sensor has been identified to date, and yeast seems to lack Sestrin and Castor proteins.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Yeast seems to lack Sestrin and Castor proteins.
source: For instance, although Gln behaves as a key signal for sustained TORC1 stimulation (Crespo et al., 2002; Stracka et al., 2014), no Gln sensor has been identified to date, and yeast seems to lack Sestrin and Castor proteins.
evidence: This is based on current knowledge about yeast genome and protein families.

claim: No study has evidenced any particular role of vacuolar amino acid transporters in TORC1 regulation in yeast.
source: Furthermore, no study has evidenced any particular role of vacuolar amino acid transporters in TORC1 regulation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The yeast leucyl-tRNA synthetase plays a role in sensing balanced levels of isoleucine, leucine, and valine and acts as a GEF for Gtr1.
source: The yeast leucyl-tRNA synthetase is reported to play a role in sensing balanced levels of isoleucine, leucine, and valine and to act as a GEF for Gtr1 (Bonfils et al., 2012), whereas the equivalent mammalian enzyme is proposed to control mTORC1 as a GAP for RagD (Han et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mammalian leucyl-tRNA synthetase is proposed to control mTORC1 as a GAP for RagD.
source: The yeast leucyl-tRNA synthetase is reported to play a role in sensing balanced levels of isoleucine, leucine, and valine and to act as a GEF for Gtr1 (Bonfils et al., 2012), whereas the equivalent mammalian enzyme is proposed to control mTORC1 as a GAP for RagD (Han et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: β-alanine is a substrate of the Gap1 permease.
source: We focused on beta-alanine (β-ala) and confirmed its reported status as a Gap1 substrate (Stolz and Sauer, 1999) by comparing the uptake of [14C]-β-ala (0.5 mM) in proline-grown wild-type and gap1∆ mutant cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: β-alanine cannot sustain growth when used as sole N source.
source: β-Ala, however, cannot sustain growth when used as sole N source, that is it cannot serve as a source of amino acids (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GABA can sustain growth when used as sole N source.
source: This contrasts with 4-aminobutyrate (GABA), an amino acid differing from β-ala by a single additional CH2 group (Figure 1A) and whose catabolism depends on a specific GABA transaminase (Andersen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is implied by the contrast with β-ala and supported by Figure 1A showing growth on GABA.

claim: GABA catabolism depends on a specific GABA transaminase.
source: This contrasts with 4-aminobutyrate (GABA), an amino acid differing from β-ala by a single additional CH2 group (Figure 1A) and whose catabolism depends on a specific GABA transaminase (Andersen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Addition of β-alanine causes ubiquitylation of Gap1.
source: This proved to be the case, as addition of β-ala (0.5 mM) caused the appearance, above the immunodetected Gap1 signal, of two slowly migrating bands that were not observed with the non-ubiquitylable Gap1(K9R,K16R) mutant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Upon β-alanine addition, Gap1 initially present at the cell surface undergoes endocytosis and targeting to the vacuole.
source: Upon β-ala addition, furthermore, Gap1 initially present at the cell surface underwent endocytosis and targeting to the vacuole, whereas Gap1(K9R,K16R) remained stable at the plasma membrane (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gap1(K9R,K16R) remains stable at the plasma membrane upon β-alanine addition.
source: Upon β-ala addition, furthermore, Gap1 initially present at the cell surface underwent endocytosis and targeting to the vacuole, whereas Gap1(K9R,K16R) remained stable at the plasma membrane (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An inactive Gap1 mutant (Gap1-126) fails to be ubiquitylated and downregulated upon β-alanine addition.
source: An inactive Gap1 mutant (Gap1-126) (Ghaddar et al., 2014b) failed to be ubiquitylated and downregulated upon β-ala addition (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Addition of β-alanine to proline-grown cells causes a Rap-sensitive reduction of the electrophoretic mobility of HA-tagged Npr1.
source: To our surprise, addition of β-ala to proline-grown cells caused a typical manifestation of TORC1 activation: a Rap-sensitive reduction of the electrophoretic mobility of HA-tagged Npr1, indicative of increased phosphorylation via TORC1 (Merhi and AndreAndré, 2012; Schmidt et al., 1998) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citations to previous literature.

claim: β-alanine causes a Rap-sensitive increase in the phosphorylation of Sch9 kinase residue Thr737.
source: β-Ala similarly caused a Rap-sensitive increase in the phosphorylation of Sch9 kinase residue Thr737 (Figure 1E), a known TORC1 target (Urban et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citation to previous literature.

claim: TORC1 activation by β-alanine is largely impaired in the gap1∆ mutant.
source: It thus seemed that activation of TORC1, largely impaired in the gap1∆ mutant (Figure 1D and E), could contribute to the observed β-ala-induced downregulation of Gap1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: β-alanine uptake does not increase the intracellular concentrations of individual amino acids, apart from β-alanine itself.
source: β-Ala uptake, however, was found not to increase the intracellular concentrations of individual amino acids, measured in cell extracts, apart from that of β-ala itself (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of Npr1 upon β-alanine addition is impaired in gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant cells.
source: Increased phosphorylation of Npr1 upon β-ala addition was indeed impaired in gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant cells (Figure 1G), and this effect was not due to reduced uptake of β-ala (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: Gap1-mediated uptake of β-alanine elicits TORC1 activation via the Rag GTPases.
source: We conclude that Gap1-mediated uptake of β-ala elicits TORC1 activation via the Rag GTPases, and that this effect is not due to conversion of intracellular β-ala to other amino acids.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing Gtr-dependence and lack of amino acid pool changes.

claim: Gap1 has been reported to be a 'transceptor' capable of activating protein kinase A (PKA) in a cAMP-independent manner.
source: Gap1 has been reported to be a 'transceptor', that is a protein combining the properties of transporters and receptors, capable of activating protein kinase A (PKA) in a cAMP-independent manner (Donaton et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Conformational changes of Gap1, triggered by binding and/or transport of amino acids, would stimulate a PKA-targeting signaling pathway.
source: According to this model, conformational changes of Gap1, triggered by binding and/or transport of amino acids, would stimulate a PKA-targeting signaling pathway (Schothorst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature describing the transceptor model.

claim: Gap1 interacts with Gtr2.
source: This hypothesis is potentially supported by a previous report that Gap1 interacts with Gtr2 (Gao and Kaiser, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The high-affinity proline permease Put4 catalyzes β-alanine transport.
source: Confirming a previous prediction (Gournas et al., 2015), we found the high-affinity proline permease Put4 also to catalyze β-ala transport.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous prediction and experimental data.

claim: In proline-free media, the gap1∆ mutant displays residual uptake of β-alanine, which is abolished in the gap1∆ put4∆ mutant.
source: Under these conditions, the gap1∆ mutant displayed residual uptake of β-ala (2 mM), and this uptake was abolished in the gap1∆ put4∆ mutant (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Put4-dependent β-alanine uptake is associated with Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1.
source: Importantly, this Put4-dependent β-ala uptake was associated with a Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HcGap1 shares approximately 30% sequence identity with Gap1 and Put4.
source: HcGap1 shares ~ 30% sequence identity with Gap1 and Put4.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: In proline-grown gap1∆ cells, HcGap1 restores high β-alanine uptake activity.
source: In proline-grown gap1∆ cells, HcGap1 restored high β-ala uptake activity, roughly similar to that conferred by Put4 to urea-grown cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: HcGap1-mediated uptake of β-alanine is associated with Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1.
source: Remarkably, this uptake of β-ala was also associated with Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Transport of β-alanine via endogenous Gap1 and/or Put4 or via the heterologous HcGap1 permease elicits TORC1 activation.
source: In conclusion, transport of β-ala via endogenous Gap1 and/or Put4 or via the heterologous HcGap1 permease elicits TORC1 activation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation with multiple permeases.

claim: Arginine uptake by proline-grown cells is mediated by Gap1 and the arginine-specific permease Can1.
source: Uptake of arginine (Arg) by proline-grown cells is known to be mediated by Gap1 and the arginine-specific permease Can1 (Wiame et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: High arginine uptake activity is measured in wild type and in gap1∆ and can1∆ single mutants, but none in the gap1∆ can1∆ double mutant.
source: Consistently, we measured high Arg uptake activity in the wild type and in gap1∆ and can1∆ single mutants, but none in the gap1∆ can1∆ double mutant (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Can1, in contrast to Gap1, does not stimulate PKA upon substrate transport.
source: According to a previous report, Can1, in contrast to Gap1, does not stimulate PKA upon substrate transport (Donaton et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Arginine uptake into wild-type cells induces Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation.
source: Arg uptake into wild-type cells was indeed found to induce Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Arginine-elicited TORC1 activation is impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant.
source: This response was impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant, an effect not due to decreased Arg uptake (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Arginine-elicited TORC1 activation results in Sch9 phosphorylation.
source: Arg-elicited TORC1 activation also resulted in Sch9 phosphorylation (Figure 3C), as previously reported (Stracka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and citation to previous literature.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of Npr1 upon arginine addition is detected in gap1∆ and can1∆ single mutants, but not in the gap1∆ can1∆ strain.
source: Increased phosphorylation of Npr1 upon Arg addition was also detected in gap1∆ and can1∆ single mutants, but not in the gap1∆ can1∆ strain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both Gap1 and Can1 can promote arginine-induced TORC1 activation.
source: This shows that both permeases can promote Arg-induced TORC1 activation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation in single mutants.

claim: HcGap1 expressed in the gap1∆ can1∆ strain restores high arginine uptake.
source: We next expressed HcGap1 in the gap1∆ can1∆ strain and found it to restore high Arg uptake (Figure 3D) associated with Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Arginine catabolism requires arginase (Car1).
source: Arginine catabolism requires arginase (Car1) (Wiame et al., 1985), so a car1 mutant fails to grow on Arg as sole N source (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Arginine addition to the car1 mutant results in Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation.
source: Arg addition to the car1 mutant also resulted in Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: TORC1 is activated upon arginine uptake via the endogenous Gap1 and/or Can1 or the heterologous HcGap1 permease.
source: In conclusion, TORC1 is activated upon Arg uptake via the endogenous Gap1 and/or Can1 or the heterologous HcGap1 permease.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation with multiple permeases.

claim: TORC1 activation by arginine involves the Rag GTPases and occurs even if arginine is not catabolized.
source: This activation of TORC1 involves the Rag GTPases and occurs even if Arg is not catabolized.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing Gtr-dependence and activation in car1 mutant.

claim: Gap1, Put4, Can1, and HcGap1 behave as H+-symporters.
source: Hence, as expected, all four permeases analyzed in our study, including HcGap1, behave as H+-symporters.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing FCCP and glucose starvation effects on uptake.

claim: Incubation of cells with the FCCP protonophore causes a strong reduction of β-alanine uptake via Gap1, Put4, or HcGap1.
source: In support of this view, incubation of cells with the FCCP protonophore caused a strong reduction of β-ala uptake via Gap1, Put4, or HcGap1 and of Arg uptake via Gap1, Can1, or HcGap1 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Incubation of cells with the FCCP protonophore causes a strong reduction of arginine uptake via Gap1, Can1, or HcGap1.
source: In support of this view, incubation of cells with the FCCP protonophore caused a strong reduction of β-ala uptake via Gap1, Put4, or HcGap1 and of Arg uptake via Gap1, Can1, or HcGap1 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Each permease (Gap1, Put4, Can1, HcGap1) is rapidly inhibited when cells are shifted to glucose-free medium.
source: Furthermore, each permease was rapidly inhibited when the cells were shifted to glucose-free medium (Figure 4A and B), a condition known to cause rapid inhibition of the Pma1 H+-ATPase and thus collapse of the plasma membrane H+ gradient (Kane, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B and citation to previous literature.

claim: Glucose starvation causes rapid inhibition of the Pma1 H+-ATPase and collapse of the plasma membrane H+ gradient.
source: Furthermore, each permease was rapidly inhibited when the cells were shifted to glucose-free medium (Figure 4A and B), a condition known to cause rapid inhibition of the Pma1 H+-ATPase and thus collapse of the plasma membrane H+ gradient (Kane, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Uptake of cytosine via the Fcy2 permease is coupled to H+ influx.
source: We chose cytosine, whose uptake via the Fcy2 permease is known to be coupled to H+ influx (Pinson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Addition of cytosine causes rapid activation of TORC1, as judged by increased Npr1 and Sch9 phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, addition of cytosine did cause rapid activation of TORC1, as judged by increased Npr1 and Sch9 phosphorylation (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Cytosine-elicited TORC1 activation is largely impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant.
source: Furthermore, this cytosine-elicited TORC1 activation was largely impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cytosine can be used as sole N source.
source: Cytosine can be used as sole N source, and thus as a source of amino acids.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of cytosine metabolism.

claim: In an fcy1 mutant lacking cytosine deaminase, Npr1 is still phosphorylated upon cytosine addition.
source: Yet in an fcy1 mutant lacking cytosine deaminase and thus unable to use cytosine as an N source, Npr1 was still phosphorylated upon cytosine addition, unless Rap was also present (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: H+-coupled uptake of cytosine stimulates TORC1 in a Rag/Gtr-dependent manner, even when the nucleobase is not assimilated into amino acids.
source: H+-coupled uptake of cytosine thus stimulates TORC1 in a Rag/Gtr-dependent manner, even when the nucleobase is not assimilated into amino acids.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation in fcy1 mutant.

claim: Hexoses including fructose enter cells via several Hxt transporters that function as facilitators.
source: Hexoses including fructose are known to enter cells via several Hxt transporters that function as facilitators (Wieczorke et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Particular S. cerevisiae strains express an H+-coupled specific fructose transporter called Fsy1.
source: Yet particular S. cerevisiae strains are reported to also express an H+-coupled specific fructose transporter called Fsy1 (Galeote et al., 2010; Rodrigues de Sousa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Equivalent fructose uptake is measured in Hxt- and Fsy1-expressing cells under the experimental conditions used.
source: Using these growth conditions, we measured equivalent 14C-fructose uptake in Hxt- and Fsy1-expressing cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Fructose uptake via Fsy1 is inhibited in the presence of FCCP, but uptake mediated by the Hxt facilitators is not.
source: Furthermore, fructose uptake via Fsy1 was inhibited in the presence of FCCP, but uptake mediated by the Hxt facilitators was not (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: A Rap-sensitive increase of Sch9 phosphorylation is observed upon fructose uptake by Fsy1-expressing cells.
source: We observed a Rap-sensitive increase of Sch9 phosphorylation upon fructose uptake by Fsy1-expressing cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: TORC1 activation is not observed in the wild-type incorporating fructose via the Hxt facilitators.
source: Such a TORC1 activation was observed neither in the wild-type incorporating fructose via the Hxt facilitators nor in the hxt null mutant expressing none fructose transporter (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: TORC1 activation in response to fructose uptake occurs only when this transport is coupled to H+ influx.
source: TORC1 activation in response to fructose uptake thus occurred only when this transport was coupled to H+ influx.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data comparing Fsy1 and Hxt-mediated uptake.

claim: FCCP causes the cytosolic pH to drop to about 6.1, the pH of the buffered growth medium.
source: Using a strain stably expressing pHluorin, we first observed that the ionophore caused the cytosolic pH to drop to about 6.1, the pH of the buffered growth medium (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Rapid acidification of the cytosol by FCCP coincides with hyperphosphorylation of Npr1.
source: Remarkably, this rapid acidification of the cytosol coincided with hyperphosphorylation of Npr1, and this response was inhibited by Rap (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: H+ influx mediated by a protonophore results in TORC1 stimulation.
source: Hence, H+ influx mediated by a protonophore also results in TORC1 stimulation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing Npr1 hyperphosphorylation upon FCCP treatment.

claim: TORC1 activation by FCCP does not lead to increased phosphorylation of Sch9.
source: Yet this TORC1 activation, intriguingly, did not lead to increased phosphorylation of Sch9 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When the cytosol becomes too acidic, an additional control likely impedes phosphorylation of Sch9 by activated TORC1.
source: A likely explanation is that an additional control elicited when the cytosol becomes too acidic (a stressful condition) impedes phosphorylation of Sch9 by activated TORC1.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed lack of Sch9 phosphorylation.

claim: When the cytosolic pH drops to values around 6, the action of TORC1 on Sch9 is inhibited, whereas nitrogen control of the Gat1 and Gln3 transcription factors via TORC1 remains unaltered.
source: This is in keeping with a previous report that when the cytosolic pH drops to values around 6 (as occurs under glucose starvation or when expression of the Pma1 H+-ATPase is repressed), the action of TORC1 on Sch9 is inhibited, whereas nitrogen control of the Gat1 and Gln3 transcription factors via TORC1 remains unaltered (Dechant et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TORC1 activation in response to FCCP-mediated H+ influx is largely impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ strain.
source: TORC1 activation in response to an FCCP-mediated H+ influx, thus visible on immunoblots for HA-Npr1, was largely impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ strain (Figure 5D), indicating that it is Rag/Gtr-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The multisubunit SEACIT complex antagonizes TORC1 by acting as a GAP on the Gtr1 GTPase.
source: The multisubunit SEACIT complex antagonizes TORC1 by acting as a GAP on the Gtr1 GTPase, and its function is itself negatively controlled by the multisubunit SEACAT complex (Panchaud et al., 2013a, 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TORC1 activation by FCCP is largely impaired in the seh1∆ mutant.
source: TORC1 activation was largely impaired in the seh1∆ mutant (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In the iml1∆ mutant, a high basal phosphorylation of HA-Npr1 is detected.
source: In the iml1∆ mutant, a high basal phosphorylation of HA-Npr1 was detected, as expected, and FCCP did not significantly further increase this phosphorylation, at least during the first minutes after its addition (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The SEACIT/SEACAT upstream regulators of Gtr1 are involved in H+-influx-elicited stimulation of TORC1 activity.
source: These results indicate that the SEACIT/SEACAT upstream regulators of Gtr1 are involved in H+-influx-elicited stimulation of TORC1 activity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing effects in seh1∆ and iml1∆ mutants.

claim: The amount of HA-Npr1 is much reduced in seh1∆ mutant cells.
source: We also found the amount of HA-Npr1 to be much reduced in seh1∆ mutant cells, and a similar effect though less pronounced was observed in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ strain (Figures 1G, 4E and 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The abundance of HA-Npr1 is influenced by the activation state of TORC1.
source: This suggests that the abundance of HA-Npr1 is influenced by the activation state of TORC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced HA-Npr1 in mutants with altered TORC1 activity.

claim: Phosphorylation of HA-Npr1 increases after prolonged incubation with FCCP in gtr1∆ gtr2∆, seh1∆, and iml1∆ mutants.
source: Furthermore, phosphorylation of HA-Npr1 in the above-analyzed mutants was found to increase after prolonged incubation with FCCP (Figure 5D, E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D, E, and F.

claim: FCCP stimulates another mechanism of TORC1 activation that does not depend on the Rag/Gtr GTPases.
source: It thus seems that FCCP stimulates another mechanism of TORC1 activation that does not depend on the Rag/Gtr GTPases.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of delayed TORC1 activation in Gtr mutants.

claim: The vacuole-associated Pib2 protein containing a FYVE domain acts in parallel with Gtr1 to promote TORC1 activation.
source: It has in fact been reported that the vacuole-associated Pib2 protein containing a FYVE domain acts in parallel with Gtr1 to promote TORC1 activation (Kim and Cunningham, 2015; Varlakhanova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In an in vitro TORC1 kinase assay using isolated vacuoles, the addition of glutamine stimulates TORC1 activity in a manner dependent on Pib2 but not Gtr1.
source: Furthermore, in an in vitro TORC1 kinase assay using isolated vacuoles, the addition of glutamine was found to stimulate TORC1 activity in a manner dependent on Pib2 but not Gtr1 (Tanigawa and Maeda, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: HA-Npr1 is normally hyperphosphorylated after FCCP addition to pib2∆ mutant cells.
source: We thus also analyzed the role of Pib2 and found that HA-Npr1 is normally hyperphosphorylated after FCCP addition to pib2∆ mutant cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: H+ influx mediated by a protonophore elicits a cellular response resulting in Rag/Gtr-dependent, Pib2-independent, TORC1 activation.
source: In conclusion, the above experiments indicate that H+ influx mediated even by a protonophore elicits a cellular response resulting in Rag/Gtr-dependent, Pib2-independent, TORC1 activation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing Gtr-dependence and Pib2-independence.

claim: Addition of amino acids, cytosine, or NH4+ to growing cells does not detectably change their cytosolic pH.
source: We observed that addition of amino acids, cytosine, or NH4+ to growing cells does not detectably change their cytosolic pH (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations (data not shown).

claim: The cytosol has high buffering capacity.
source: This was expected, given the high buffering capacity of the cytosol and the compensating H+ efflux activity of the Pma1 H+-ATPase, which is stimulated under acidic conditions as long as glucose is present (Eraso and Gancedo, 1987; Ullah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on cytosolic buffering.

claim: The Pma1 H+-ATPase is stimulated under acidic conditions as long as glucose is present.
source: This was expected, given the high buffering capacity of the cytosol and the compensating H+ efflux activity of the Pma1 H+-ATPase, which is stimulated under acidic conditions as long as glucose is present (Eraso and Gancedo, 1987; Ullah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The vacuolar V-ATPase catalyzes ATP-dependent uptake of H+ into the vacuole to acidify the organelle, compensate for constant H+ efflux, and control cytosolic pH.
source: An H+ increase can in principle be caused by inhibition of the vacuolar V-ATPase, as this enzymatic complex catalyzes ATP-dependent uptake of H+ into the vacuole in order to acidify the organelle, to compensate for the constant H+ efflux mediated by H+-coupled vacuolar transporters, and to control the cytosolic pH (Kane, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on V-ATPase function.

claim: Addition of concanamycin A (CMA) to proline-grown cells does not significantly change the cytosolic pH.
source: Addition of CMA to proline-grown cells did not significantly change the cytosolic pH of the cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pma1-dependent efflux and the buffering capacity of the cytosol prevent the expected increase in cytosolic H+ upon CMA treatment.
source: This suggests that Pma1-dependent efflux and the buffering capacity of the cytosol prevented the expected increase in cytosolic H+.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of pH change despite V-ATPase inhibition.

claim: BAF addition causes a slight but significant drop in the cytosolic pH.
source: BAF addition did cause a slight but significant drop in the cytosolic pH, suggesting that this treatment caused stronger inhibition of the V-ATPase (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Both CMA and BAF treatment result in stimulation of TORC1 activity, as judged by Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1.
source: Remarkably, both CMA and BAF treatment resulted in stimulation of TORC1 activity, as judged by Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 (Figure 6B and Figure 6F, respectively) and by a transient increase in Sch9 phosphorylation (Figure 6C and Figure 6G, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6B, 6C, 6F, and 6G.

claim: No increase in Npr1 phosphorylation is detected in either CMA- or BAF-treated gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant cells.
source: No increase in Npr1 phosphorylation was detected in either CMA- or BAF-treated gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant cells (Figure 6D and H, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D and 6H.

claim: Inhibition of the V-ATPase is associated with efficient Rag/Gtr-dependent stimulation of TORC1 activity.
source: We conclude that inhibition of the V-ATPase is associated with efficient Rag/Gtr-dependent stimulation of TORC1 activity, even when this inhibition is not sufficient to cause a detectable lowering of the cytosolic pH.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation by V-ATPase inhibitors.

claim: Several plant H+-ATPases are active when expressed in yeast strains where PMA1 and PMA2 are deleted or repressed.
source: According to previous reports, several plant H+-ATPases are active when expressed in yeast strains where the essential PMA1 gene and its non-essential paralog PMA2 (expressed to a much lower level) are deleted or repressed (Morsomme et al., 2000; Palmgren and Christensen, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Wild-type forms of plant H+-ATPases typically compensate only partially for the lack of Pma1.
source: The wild-type forms of these plant H+-ATPases typically compensate only partially for the lack of Pma1.
evidence: This is based on previous literature on plant H+-ATPase expression in yeast.

claim: It is possible to isolate mutant derivatives of plant H+-ATPases sustaining faster growth, particularly on low-pH media.
source: It is possible, however, to isolate mutant derivatives sustaining faster growth, particularly on low-pH media where cells need high H+-ATPase activity to maintain a neutral cytosolic pH (Morsomme et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The H+-ATPase Pma4 of tobacco restores limited growth to a pma1∆ pma2∆ double-null mutant.
source: For instance, the H+-ATPase Pma4 of tobacco (Nicotiana plumbaginifolia) restores limited growth to a pma1∆ pma2∆ double-null mutant.
evidence: This is based on previous literature on plant H+-ATPase expression in yeast.

claim: A truncated Pma4 protein called Pma4882ochre, lacking the last 71 C-terminal amino acids, is able to support faster growth of yeast pma1∆ pma2∆ cells.
source: A truncated Pma4 protein called Pma4882ochre, lacking the last 71 C-terminal amino acids as a result of an ochre nonsense mutation in codon 882 of the PMA4 gene, is able to support faster growth of yeast pma1∆ pma2∆ cells (Luo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cells expressing PMA4822ochre grow more slowly than cells expressing PMA1.
source: We found cells expressing PMA4822ochre to grow more slowly (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The mutant plant H+-ATPase does not fully compensate for the lack of Pma1.
source: This shows that the mutant plant H+-ATPase does not fully compensate for the lack of Pma1.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the growth data.

claim: The cytosolic pH of PMA4822ochre-expressing cells is slightly lower than that of PMA1-expressing cells.
source: Accordingly, compared to the cytosolic pH of PMA1-expressing cells, that of PMA4822ochre-expressing cells was slightly lower (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: H+-coupled uptake of β-alanine is significantly lower in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells compared to PMA1-expressing cells.
source: H+-coupled uptake of β-ala (1 mM) was also significantly lower in the latter cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations (data not shown).

claim: β-alanine uptake is coupled to H+ influx in both PMA1- and PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.
source: As expected, and whichever gene was expressed, [14C]-β-ala uptake was inhibited after a brief treatment of the cells with FCCP. This shows that in both cases, β-ala uptake is coupled to H+ influx (Figure 7D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7D and 7F.

claim: Upon transfer to glucose-free medium, uptake of β-alanine into PMA1-expressing cells is strongly reduced.
source: Upon transfer of the cells to a glucose-free medium, uptake of β-ala into PMA1-expressing cells was also strongly reduced (Figure 7D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7D and 7F.

claim: The reduction in β-alanine uptake upon glucose starvation is much less pronounced in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.
source: This reduction was much less pronounced in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells (Figure 7D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7D and 7F.

claim: Inactivation of H+-ATPases upon glucose starvation requires a C-terminal auto-inhibitory region which the truncated protein Pma4822ochre lacks.
source: This result can be readily explained by the fact that inactivation of H+-ATPases upon glucose starvation, a regulation conserved between yeast and plant H+-ATPases, requires a C-terminal auto-inhibitory region which the truncated protein Pma4822ochre lacks (Morsomme et al., 2000; Portillo, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on H+-ATPase regulation.

claim: Phosphorylation of Npr1 increases moderately upon addition of β-alanine at low concentration to PMA1-expressing cells.
source: Phosphorylation of Npr1 was found to increase moderately upon addition of β-ala at low concentration (0.1 mM) to PMA1-expressing cells, but this variation was significant, as judged by its sensitivity to Rap (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: No increase in Npr1 phosphorylation is detected in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells upon β-alanine addition.
source: Remarkably, no increase in Npr1 phosphorylation was detected in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Basal phosphorylation of Npr1 in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells does not increase, despite the lower pH of their cytosol.
source: Furthermore, basal phosphorylation of Npr1 in these cells did not increase, despite the lower pH of their cytosol (Figure 7E and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7E and 7C.

claim: Non-activation of TORC1 in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells upon β-alanine uptake is even clearer when Sch9 phosphorylation is used as readout.
source: Non-activation of TORC1 in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells was even clearer when Sch9 phosphorylation was used as readout (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Basal phosphorylation of Sch9 before β-alanine addition is reduced in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.
source: Basal phosphorylation of Sch9 before β-ala addition was also reduced in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: FCCP addition causes a rapid drop in the cytosolic pH in both PMA1- and PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.
source: In both PMA1- and PMA4822ochre-expressing cells, as expected, the ionophore caused a rapid drop in the cytosolic pH, to a value close to the pH of the buffered external medium (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: FCCP addition induces strong hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 in control PMA1-expressing cells.
source: Also as expected, this induced strong hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 in control PMA1-expressing cells (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: FCCP addition does not increase Npr1 phosphorylation in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.
source: In contrast, FCCP addition did not increase Npr1 phosphorylation in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Npr1 phosphorylation increases in PMA1-expressing but not in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells after treatment with BAF.
source: Similar results were obtained after treatment with BAF: Npr1 phosphorylation was found to increase in PMA1-expressing but not in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The endogenous Pma1 H+-ATPase plays an essential role in Rag/Gtr-dependent TORC1 activation in response to increased cytosolic H+.
source: These results show that the endogenous Pma1 H+-ATPase plays an essential role in Rag/Gtr-dependent TORC1 activation in response to increased cytosolic H+.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data comparing PMA1- and PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.

claim: PMA1-expressing cells can resume growth following exposure to Rap, whereas PMA4822ochre-expressing cells fail to do so.
source: The importance of Pma1 in stimulating TORC1 activity was also illustrated by the ability of PMA1-expressing cells to resume growth following exposure to Rap, whereas PMA4822ochre-expressing cells failed to do so (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The Rag GTPases are not required for sustained activation of TORC1 in the presence of NH4+.
source: It has been reported that the Rag GTPases are not required for sustained activation of TORC1 in the presence of NH4+ (Stracka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: NH4+ addition to proline-grown cells causes Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 in both wild-type and gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant cells.
source: In support of this view, NH4+ addition to proline-grown cells caused Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 in both wild-type and gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant cells (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Sustained TORC1 activation after NH4+ addition depends on the enzymes converting NH4+ to glutamate.
source: Furthermore, sustained TORC1 activation after NH4+ addition is reported to depend on the enzymes converting NH4+ to glutamate (Fayyad-Kazan et al., 2016; Merhi and AndreAndré, 2012), the main N donor in amino acid biogenesis reactions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Upon NH4+ addition to proline-grown cells, TORC1 is properly activated regardless of the H+-ATPase produced (Pma1 or Pma4822ochre).
source: Interestingly, upon NH4+ addition to proline-grown cells, we found TORC1 to be properly activated by NH4+ regardless of the H+-ATPase produced (Pma1 or the plant Pma4822ochre) (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: TORC1 can be properly activated in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.
source: This result shows that TORC1 can be properly activated in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the NH4+ activation data.

claim: Pma1 is required for TORC1 activation in response to H+ influx but not to an increase in internal amino acids.
source: It also suggests that Pma1 is required for TORC1 activation in response to H+ influx but not to an increase in internal amino acids.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential requirement for Pma1 in different activation conditions.

claim: What triggers TORC1 activation upon amino acid uptake is the H+ influx coupled to transport by H+/amino-acid symporters.
source: Our study shows that what triggers this activation is the H+ influx coupled to transport by H+/amino-acid symporters.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: A similar TORC1 activation response is observed upon H+-dependent uptake of cytosine or fructose.
source: A similar response is observed upon H+-dependent uptake of cytosine, or even fructose, but not when an equivalent amount of fructose enters the cells via passive transport systems.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on cytosine and fructose uptake.

claim: The activation of TORC1 can be elicited by diffusion of extracellular H+ via a protonophore.
source: The activation of TORC1 can even be elicited by diffusion of extracellular H+ via a protonophore or by inactivation of the vacuolar V-ATPase (which also causes an increase in cytosolic H+).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on FCCP treatment.

claim: The activation of TORC1 can be elicited by inactivation of the vacuolar V-ATPase.
source: The activation of TORC1 can even be elicited by diffusion of extracellular H+ via a protonophore or by inactivation of the vacuolar V-ATPase (which also causes an increase in cytosolic H+).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on V-ATPase inhibitor treatment.

claim: TORC1 activation in response to H+ influx and/or an increase in cytosolic H+ requires the Rag GTPases encoded by the GTR genes.
source: We further show that TORC1 activation in response to an H+ influx and/or an increase in cytosolic H+ requires the Rag GTPases encoded by the GTR genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing impaired activation in gtr mutants.

claim: TORC1 activation in response to H+ influx does not require the Pib2 protein.
source: It does not, however, require the Pib2 protein recently shown to act in parallel with the Rag/Gtr proteins to activate TORC1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing normal activation in pib2∆ mutant.

claim: The Pma1 H+-ATPase plays a central role in TORC1 activation in response to H+ influx.
source: Finally, we show that the Pma1 H+-ATPase plays a central role in this TORC1 activation pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing cells expressing Pma1 versus plant H+-ATPase.

claim: Yeast cells typically adapt to starvation for any nutrient by reducing TORC1 activity.
source: Yeast cells typically adapt to starvation for any nutrient by reducing TORC1 activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast cell responses to starvation.

claim: Mechanisms capable of sensing the nutritional status of the cell impede the activation of TORC1 during starvation.
source: This is probably because mechanisms capable of sensing the nutritional status of the cell impede the activation of TORC1, and not just because of a possible drop in H+-coupled uptake of this nutrient.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for TORC1 inhibition during starvation.

claim: Reduction of TORC1 activity during starvation typically coincides with increased synthesis of large amounts of high-affinity H+-symporters.
source: This reduction of TORC1 activity typically coincides with increased synthesis of large amounts of high-affinity H+-symporters able to assimilate replenishing compounds, for example, Gap1 for amino acids, Pho84 for phosphate, Sul1 and Sul2 for sulfate, Zrt1 for zinc, Fcy2 for cytosine, and Fur4 for uracil.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast responses to starvation.

claim: Many permeases for non-limiting nutrients likely undergo increased endocytosis and degradation during starvation.
source: Furthermore, many permeases for the non-limiting nutrients likely undergo parallel increased endocytosis and degradation, as such responses have been observed in rapamycin-treated cells (Crapeau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Permease reconfiguration at the plasma membrane during starvation probably causes an overall reduction of H+ influx.
source: This permease reconfiguration at the plasma membrane probably causes an overall reduction of the H+ influx.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the changes in permease expression.

claim: H+-symporters that are derepressed under starvation conditions are potentially able to reactivate TORC1 once their substrate becomes available again.
source: Our results suggest that the H+-symporters that are derepressed under starvation conditions are potentially able to reactivate TORC1 once their substrate becomes available again in the medium.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: H+ influx via H+-symporters could provide a general signal for reactivating TORC1 upon relief from diverse starvation conditions.
source: In other words, H+ influx via these transporters could provide a general signal for reactivating TORC1 upon relief from diverse starvation conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the results.

claim: Sustained activation of TORC1 probably requires efficient assimilation of the internalized nutrient.
source: On the other hand, sustained activation of TORC1 probably requires efficient assimilation of the internalized nutrient.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on previous knowledge.

claim: Longer term TORC1 activation after addition of NH4+ requires glutamine accumulation and/or synthesis.
source: Accordingly, longer term TORC1 activation after addition of a preferential N source such as NH4+ is reported to require glutamine accumulation and/or synthesis (Stracka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The influx of H+ coupled to uptake of any growth-limiting nutrient might provide a general signal for rapid, transient TORC1 reactivation.
source: The influx of H+ coupled to uptake of any growth-limiting nutrient might thus provide a general signal for rapid, transient TORC1 reactivation in order to prepare cells for subsequent growth acceleration or restart once the nutrient has been properly assimilated.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the results.

claim: H+ influx could contribute to the reactivation of TORC1 upon addition of glucose to glucose-starved cells.
source: It could also contribute to the reactivation of TORC1 observed upon addition of glucose to glucose-starved cells, as although glucose enters cells via Hxt facilitators it also reactivates Pma1, which in turn drives the H+-coupled uptake of amino acids and other nutrients.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for TORC1 reactivation upon glucose addition.

claim: Uptake of amino acids by N-starved cells elicits transient activation of PKA, resulting in stimulation of trehalase by phosphorylation.
source: Uptake of amino acids by N-starved cells is also reported to elicit transient activation of PKA, resulting in stimulation of trehalase by phosphorylation (Donaton et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: PKA could be activated via a signaling pathway stimulated by Gap1 acting as a transceptor.
source: According to current models, PKA could be activated via a signaling pathway stimulated by Gap1 acting as a transceptor, and a similar function has been described for other H+-coupled nutrient transporters found to be derepressed under particular starvation conditions (Schothorst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on the transceptor model.

claim: The signal eliciting PKA activation might be the H+ influx coupled to the nutrient uptake reaction.
source: It is tempting to envisage an alternative model according to which the signal eliciting PKA activation is the H+ influx coupled to the nutrient uptake reaction, as in the case of TORC1.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Addition of FCCP to N-starved cells results in stimulation of trehalase activity.
source: This model is worth considering, since addition of FCCP to N-starved cells results in stimulation of trehalase activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of excess glutamine to proline-grown cells causes a rapid, transient activation of TORC1, not observed in the gtr1∆ mutant.
source: In a previous study, addition of excess Gln to proline-grown cells was found to cause a rapid, transient activation of TORC1, not observed in the gtr1∆ mutant, followed by a more sustained TORC1 activity, still observed in gtr1∆ cells (Stracka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Gtr1-independent TORC1 activation by glutamine is reminiscent of the situation in mouse cells, where glutamine activates mTORC1 independently of RagA and RagB.
source: This Gtr1-independent TORC1 activation is reminiscent of the situation described in mouse cells, where Gln activates mTORC1 in a manner independent of RagA and RagB (Jewell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Direct addition of glutamine to isolated vacuoles elicits TORC1 activation in vitro in a Gtr1-independent manner.
source: Similarly, direct addition of Gln to isolated vacuoles elicits TORC1 activation in vitro in a Gtr1-independent manner (Tanigawa and Maeda, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Glutamine-elicited TORC1 activation in isolated vacuoles requires the Pib2 protein.
source: In contrast, this response requires the Pib2 protein proposed to act in parallel with Gtr1 to activate TORC1 (Kim and Cunningham, 2015; Varlakhanova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Glutamine uptake first elicits a transient, Gtr1-dependent activation of TORC1, with the signal being the H+ influx coupled to glutamine transport.
source: These observations suggest that Gln uptake first elicits a transient, Gtr1-dependent activation of TORC1, and we propose that the signal of this early activation is the H+ influx coupled to Gln transport.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the results and previous literature.

claim: The subsequent sustained activation of TORC1 by glutamine is promoted by the intracellular accumulation of glutamine.
source: The subsequent sustained activation of TORC1, in contrast, is suggested to be promoted by the intracellular accumulation of Gln (Stracka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Sustained TORC1 activation occurs normally after glutamine addition to gtr1∆ cells.
source: The same applies to Gtr1/2 because, while sustained TORC1 activation occurs normally after Gln addition to gtr1∆ cells (Stracka et al., 2014), we failed to observe it in the double gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant, in keeping with another study (Varlakhanova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and the authors' own observations.

claim: Sch9 is stimulated by TORC1 in response to an increase in cytosolic H+.
source: We have found the Sch9 kinase to be stimulated by TORC1 in response to an increase in cytosolic H+.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the study.

claim: Sch9 contributes to pH homeostasis by controlling the assembly and activity of the vacuolar V-ATPase.
source: This observation is interesting, in the light of the recent finding that Sch9 contributes to pH homeostasis by controlling the assembly and activity of the vacuolar V-ATPase (Wilms et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The vacuolar V-ATPase, together with the plasma membrane H+-ATPase, contributes importantly to controlling the cytosolic pH.
source: This is relevant because the latter, together with the plasma membrane H+-ATPase, contributes importantly to controlling the cytosolic pH (Kane, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Sch9 phosphorylation and cell growth are reduced when the cytosol becomes acidic.
source: Yet according to other reports, Sch9 phosphorylation and cell growth are reduced when the cytosol becomes acidic (e.g. after a drop to a pH near 6), for instance under glucose starvation or when Pma1 synthesis is reduced (Dechant et al., 2014; Orij et al., 2012; Ullah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Even though Sch9 is activated by an H+ influx and/or by an increase in cytosolic H+, it is inhibited when the cytosol becomes too acidic.
source: It thus seems that even though Sch9 is activated by an H+ influx and/or by an increase in cytosolic H+, it is inhibited when the cytosol becomes too acidic, and this causes growth inhibition.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the experimental observations and previous literature.

claim: A particular mechanism sensitive to acidic conditions hampers Sch9 phosphorylation by activated TORC1 in FCCP-treated cells.
source: In FCCP-treated cells, accordingly, TORC1 appears to be efficiently activated (as judged by hyperphosphorylation of the Npr1 kinase), but this is not accompanied by Sch9 phosphorylation. This suggests that a particular mechanism sensitive to acidic conditions hampers Sch9 phosphorylation by activated TORC1.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed dissociation between TORC1 activation and Sch9 phosphorylation.

claim: Acidification of the cytosol is stressful for the cell and stimulation of growth under these conditions would be inappropriate.
source: Such a control seems physiologically relevant, as acidification of the cytosol is stressful for the cell and stimulation of growth under these conditions would be inappropriate.
evidence: This is a logical interpretation of the physiological significance of the observed regulation.

claim: Other stresses promote dephosphorylation of Sch9 without affecting the TORC1-regulated Tap42-PP2A branch controlling Npr1 phosphorylation.
source: Accordingly, other stresses are reported to promote dephosphorylation of Sch9 without affecting the TORC1-regulated Tap42-PP2A branch controlling Npr1 phosphorylation (Hughes Hallett et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Non-activation of TORC1 in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells might result indirectly from the inability of Pma4822ochre to fully compensate for the lack of Pma1 activity.
source: On the one hand, non-activation of TORC1 might result indirectly from the inability of Pma4822ochre to fully compensate for the lack of Pma1 activity.
evidence: This is one possible explanation considered by the authors.

claim: In PMA4822ochre-expressing cells, the cytosol is slightly acidic and cells grow more slowly.
source: We did find PMA4822ochre -expressing cells to grow more slowly and their cytosol to be slightly acidic.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the study.

claim: Slightly acidic cytosol in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells might trigger adaptive feedback mechanisms impeding TORC1 reactivation.
source: This might trigger adaptive feedback mechanisms impeding TORC1 reactivation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed lack of TORC1 activation.

claim: The essential role of Pma1 in TORC1 activation in response to H+ influx might reflect the ability of Pma1 to stimulate a signaling pathway controlling TORC1 activity.
source: Alternatively, the essential role of Pma1 in TORC1 activation in response to H+ influx might reflect the ability of Pma1 to stimulate a signaling pathway controlling TORC1 activity.
evidence: This is an alternative model proposed by the authors.

claim: The activity of Pma1 increases when the concentration of H+ in the cytosol rises, involving a decreased Km for ATP.
source: For instance, the activity of Pma1 is known to increase when the concentration of H+ in the cytosol rises, and this control involves a decreased Km for ATP (Eraso and Gancedo, 1987; Ullah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on Pma1 regulation.

claim: Pma1 activity increase likely occurs when protons are co-transported with nutrients via plasma membrane H+-symporters.
source: This activity increase also likely occurs when protons are co-transported with nutrients via plasma membrane H+-symporters.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the known properties of Pma1.

claim: Stimulation of Pma1 activity, possibly involving a conformational change, might be transmitted to cytosolic factors that would modulate TORC1 activity.
source: This stimulation of Pma1 activity, possibly involving a conformational change of the H+-ATPase, might be transmitted to cytosolic factors that would in turn modulate TORC1 activity.
evidence: This is a speculative model for how Pma1 might signal to TORC1.

claim: A role of Pma1 in signaling to TORC1 is attractive because Pma1 is the main ATP-consuming enzyme of yeast and is ideally positioned for sensing cellular ATP levels.
source: A role of Pma1 in signaling to TORC1 is attractive, because Pma1 is the main ATP-consuming enzyme of yeast and is thus ideally positioned for sensing cellular ATP levels.
evidence: This is a logical argument supporting the proposed model.

claim: Pma1 stimulation by H+ influx could give cells a general mechanism for sensing relief from starvation for any nutrient and for reactivating TORC1.
source: Furthermore, as mentioned above, Pma1 stimulation by H+ influx could also give cells a general mechanism for sensing relief from starvation for any nutrient and for reactivating TORC1 in response to this relief.
evidence: This is a speculative model for the physiological role of Pma1 in TORC1 regulation.

claim: TORC1 inhibition has been observed when Pma1 synthesis is reduced.
source: For instance, TORC1 inhibition has been observed when Pma1 synthesis is reduced (Dechant et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Yeast TORC1 is rapidly inhibited under glucose starvation, coinciding with polymerization of the kinase complex into a single, vacuole-associated cylindrical structure.
source: Furthermore, yeast TORC1 is rapidly inhibited under glucose starvation (Urban et al., 2007), this coinciding with polymerization of the kinase complex into a single, vacuole-associated cylindrical structure (Prouteau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A specific mechanism involving phosphorylation of the Kog1 subunit contributes to TORC1 inhibition under glucose starvation.
source: Although a specific mechanism involving phosphorylation of the Kog1 subunit is reported to contribute to this TORC1 inhibition (Hughes Hallett et al., 2015), a role of Pma1 might also be considered, as this H+-ATPase is subject to rapid and reversible auto-inhibition under these conditions (Portillo et al., 1989; Serrano, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pma1 is subject to rapid and reversible auto-inhibition under glucose starvation conditions.
source: Although a specific mechanism involving phosphorylation of the Kog1 subunit is reported to contribute to this TORC1 inhibition (Hughes Hallett et al., 2015), a role of Pma1 might also be considered, as this H+-ATPase is subject to rapid and reversible auto-inhibition under these conditions (Portillo et al., 1989; Serrano, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TORC1 has been reported to be required for full activity of Pma1.
source: Interestingly, TORC1 has been reported recently to be required for full activity of Pma1 (Mahmoud et al., 2017), suggesting the existence of some crosstalk between Pma1 and TORC1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The Na+/K+-ATPase of animal cells is engaged in dynamic interactions with other proteins, including the Src tyrosine kinase.
source: The model according to which Pma1 is capable of controlling TORC1 via signaling also seems reasonable in the light of previous works showing that the Na+/K+-ATPase of animals cells, a P-type ATPase structurally similar to Pma1 and other H+-ATPases, is engaged in dynamic interactions with other proteins, including the Src tyrosine kinase.
evidence: This is supported by general knowledge about Na+/K+-ATPase function.

claim: The interaction of Na+/K+-ATPase with Src is modulated by the conformation of the ion pump and initiates signal transduction processes.
source: The interaction with Src is modulated by the conformation of the ion pump and initiates signal transduction processes (Cui and Xie, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The cytosolic region of the Na+/K+-ATPase interacting directly with Src is relatively well conserved in the yeast H+-ATPase.
source: As the cytosolic region of the Na+/K+-ATPase interacting directly with Src (Lai et al., 2013) is relatively well conserved in the yeast H+-ATPase, we introduced several substitutions into this region of Pma1 with a view of disrupting possible interactions with other factors.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and sequence comparison.

claim: Pma1 variants with substitutions in the region potentially interacting with other factors behaved normally in TORC1 activation assays.
source: The generated Pma1 variants, however, behaved normally in TORC1 activation assays.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations by the authors.
